procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 16 August, 1966 passed by the Sessions Judge Sholapur.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant appealed to the Bombay High Court, Criminal Appeal No. 1444 of 1966, against the judgment and order of the Sessions Judge Sholapur. The High Court dismissed the appeal in limine (summarily) on December 5, 1966. The High Court also refused leave to appeal to the Supreme Court on April 3, 1967.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave (Criminal Appeal No. 180 of 1967) after the High Court dismissed his appeal and refused leave to appeal. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order of dismissal, and remitted the matter back to the High Court for fresh consideration after hearing the parties.

issue.issue_text: Whether it is proper for a High Court to summarily dismiss a criminal appeal in limine when it involves substantial and arguable questions of law and fact.

facts: An appellant, convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment by a Sessions Court, appealed to the High Court.
The appeal raised several substantial and arguable questions of both law and fact.
The High Court dismissed the appeal summarily, in limine (at the outset), with a single-word order.
This made it impossible to know the reasons that persuaded the High Court to dismiss the appeal.
law: Under Section 410 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, there is a right to appeal a sentence from a Sessions Court on matters of both fact and law.
While an appellate court, like the High Court, has the power to dismiss an appeal summarily, this power is not absolute.

Citing precedent (Chittaranjan Das v. State of West Bengal), the Supreme Court affirmed the principle that a High Court should not summarily reject a criminal appeal if it raises arguable and substantial points.
When an appeal involving such points is rejected, the High Court should provide reasons for its decision.
application: The Supreme Court found that the appellant's case involved substantial and arguable questions.
By dismissing the appeal with a single word, the High Court failed to provide any reasons for its decision.
This action was contrary to the established legal principle that appeals with arguable points should not be dismissed summarily without a reasoned order.
The High Court's summary dismissal prevented a proper review of the substantial questions of law and fact raised by the appellant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that it is improper for a High Court to summarily dismiss a criminal appeal in limine when it involves substantial and arguable questions. The Court held that in such cases, the High Court must consider the points raised and, if it dismisses the appeal, provide reasons for doing so. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's dismissal order and sent the case back for a fresh hearing on its merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court is required to provide reasons when dismissing a criminal appeal.

facts: An appellant, convicted by a Sessions Court and sentenced to life imprisonment, appealed to the High Court.
The appeal raised what were described as "various arguable and substantial questions of law and fact."
The High Court dismissed the appeal summarily ("in limine") with a single word, providing no reasons for its decision.
law: Under Section 410 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, there is a right to appeal a sentence from a Court of Sessions on matters of both fact and law.
While an appellate court, like the High Court, has the power to dismiss an appeal summarily, this power is not absolute.
The key legal principle established is that if a criminal appeal raises "arguable and substantial points," the High Court is required to provide reasons for its rejection.
application: The Court noted that in this specific case, the High Court's dismissal with a single word made it "not possible to know the reasons which persuaded the High Court to dismiss the appeal."
The Court reasoned that rejecting an appeal in this manner "causes difficulties and embarrassment" in understanding the basis for the decision.
Because the appeal raised substantial and arguable points, the High Court should not have dismissed it summarily without providing its reasoning.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court is required to provide reasons when dismissing a criminal appeal that raises arguable and substantial points. The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's summary dismissal, and sent the case back to the High Court for fresh consideration.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When an appeal raises arguable and substantial points, the High Court must provide reasons for its rejection.
obiter: What constitutes an arguable and substantial point may be illustrated with reference to other decisions.
An appellant is entitled to canvass every point in their favour before the High Court, including questions of fact.
A case of being heard as required under section 479A of the Criminal Procedure Code would be an arguable point.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While an appellate court, such as the High Court, possesses the power to summarily dismiss an appeal, this power is not absolute. It is improper for a High Court to summarily reject a criminal appeal in limine if the appeal raises arguable and substantial points of law or fact. In such cases, the High Court is obligated to provide reasons for its decision to reject the appeal, as a dismissal with a single word makes it impossible for a higher court to ascertain the reasoning and causes difficulties.
legal_tests_applied: Whether an appeal raises 'arguable and substantial points' is the determinative test for whether it can be summarily dismissed. If it does, it should not be summarily rejected.
If an appeal raising arguable and substantial points is to be rejected, the High Court must provide reasons for its decision.
policy_considerations: Rejection of an appeal by using only one word of dismissal causes difficulties and embarrassment in finding out the reasons which weighed with the High Court in dismissal of the appeal in limine.
